tip: For a 'would' in reported speech, French uses the conditional: 'il viendrait' = he would come. It's the future seen from a past moment.
After 'être' the past form agrees in writing only: 'est montée' adds an -e for she, but it sounds exactly like 'monté'.
'Ressembler' always takes 'à' – you resemble to someone: 'ressemblait à son père'. English 'looks like him' goes straight to the person; French adds 'à'.
The imparfait 'vendions' covers English 'used to sell' – a repeated past habit. No extra words needed; the tense alone carries the used-to.
'Le long de' means along – literally 'the length of': 'le long de la rivière'. It's a fixed three-word unit, always ending in 'de'.
French often turns a noun into an adverb with 'avec': 'avec impatience' = impatiently. Common even where a '-ment' adverb like 'impatiemment' exists.
'Vendredi dernier' (last Friday) – 'dernier' goes after days/months: 'lundi dernier', 'le mois dernier'.
'Être' builds its own past with 'avoir', not itself: 'il a été malade' = he was sick. Never 'il est été'.
'Son' agrees with the thing owned, not the owner: 'son parapluie' is her umbrella here as easily as his. The gender follows 'parapluie'.
Drop the article before a job: 'il a été professeur' = he was a teacher, with no 'un'. The profession behaves like an adjective after 'être'.
French 'makes' attention rather than paying it: 'faire attention' = to pay attention or to be careful.
'Il y avait' is simply the past of 'il y a' (there is): 'il y avait du monde' = there were people. One fixed phrase, not a verb to conjugate.
'Il faisait beau' describes the background weather; 'nous avons quitté' marks the completed event. Classic imparfait + passé composé pairing.
'Passer' flips helpers by meaning: 'être' for moving through ('nous sommes passés par...'), but 'avoir' for spending time – 'j'ai passé une semaine'.
'Sans arrêt' (non-stop) underlines that the rain just kept going – a classic cue for the imparfait 'pleuvait'.
'Sortir' uses 'être': 'elle est sortie', with an extra -e to agree with the feminine subject.
'Jouer' forms the passé composé with 'avoir': 'ils ont joué'. Only a small group of verbs, mostly movement and change, takes 'être'.
'Ils sont morts' looks like 'they are dead' but it's the past of 'mourir': 'they died'. 'Mourir' takes 'être'.
'À cette époque' (back then) is a cue for the imparfait: 'travaillait' paints how life was, not a single finished event.
Weather descriptions in the past usually use the imparfait: 'il neigeait', 'il pleuvait', 'il faisait froid'.
'Ils devaient' = they were supposed to, leaving it open whether they did. 'Ils ont dû' would mean they had to and actually did.
A small set of movement verbs like 'aller' takes 'être', not 'avoir': 'nous sommes allés' = we went. Most other verbs use 'avoir'.
English 'had been raining' is just imparfait + 'depuis' in French: 'il pleuvait depuis deux heures' = it had been raining for two hours.
'Il faisait beau' – weather in the past usually uses imparfait because it describes a backdrop/state.
French drops 'a' before a job: 'il était médecin', not 'un médecin'. Same for any profession after 'être' – 'elle est avocate', 'il est prof'.
Luck is something you have in French, not something you are: 'avons eu beaucoup de chance' = had a lot of luck, so 'we were very lucky'.
'La vaisselle' is singular – all the dishes as one heap. The usual verb is 'faire': 'faire la vaisselle', literally do the dishware.
You don't 'make' a decision in French, you take one: 'a pris une décision'. It's 'prendre', not 'faire', that goes with 'décision'.
A strong espresso is 'serré' – literally tight or squeezed. 'Un café bien serré' packs the same coffee into less water.
Reporting a future from the past? French uses the conditional: 'ils viendraient' = they would come. Said back then, it still points forward.
